Andy McDowell (ZIP code: 11222) To Whom It may Concern, While you consider granting an upzoning to the Gotham Monitor Point project, please consider the community that has been here fighting to protect our waterfront. At the time, the city and the and the property owners were framing it as a choice between waste transfer stations and oil depots or high rise apartment buildings. We were supposed to be happy that waste transfer stations would not return, despite the alternative being the essential theft of our waterfront and sky by real estate developers. Now the framing is that we need this development for "affordable" housing and to pay for Box St Park, etc. There are plenty more sites for developers to make money and also build affordable housing. Bloomberg’s rezoning plan, which ignored the neighborhood’s thorough rezoning recommendations, was a massive giveaway to moneyed real estate interests. Many of these players, with strong connections to the Bloomberg administration, bought large industrial waterfront tracts which overnight went from a value of $10M to $150M, once the Bloomberg rezoning was pushed through. Bushwick Inlet Park has come together, but at a very high cost. This is not just accounting for the staggering number of ... $500M (!!) that this park will have cost, but of the extreme community fight required to push this boulder up the hill. The battle has lasted decades, with endless advocacy invested in this very important part of our community. And now we have this waterfront green space in view, not just viable, but well underway, and behold - we are faced with the biggest of turds, ready to be laid at the very edge of our inlet, right on our park. This is an outright kick in the teeth to the entire community. Worse yet - this is proposed to happen on city owned land!!! Honestly, despite the fact that over the years while we fought for our park, groves of high rise apartment building have sprung up to steal our sky and waterfront, this particular proposal is a far more grotesque disregard for community, for this investment of effort. Any of these bonuses is important in its own right, but we should not be lured into terrible deals by shiny objects. The long view is necessary. And, though we have unwisely squandered the opportunity to responsibly develop a great proportion of the Williamsburg and Greenpoint Waterfront, we can not give up now and say “Oh, what’s another high rise on the waterfront.” This entire conflict needs to be reframed. Never say never about our ability to do great things without real estate developer perks. It might take time but we can get it done. Period.

Sean Cahill (ZIP code: 11222) The proposed upzoning of 40 Quay Street—Monitor Point—is a blatant transfer of public land to a private developer seeking to build three luxury towers just 50 feet from the Bushwick Inlet shoreline. These towers, reaching up to 56 stories, directly contradict the 2005 rezoning agreement, which promised this area would serve as a buffer zone to protect the community and transition into parkland. The developer’s plan even requests the removal of a park designation from an adjacent lot, effectively stealing public parkland to expand private luxury development. Community members strongly oppose the project on environmental, equity, and infrastructure grounds. The Bushwick Inlet is one of the East River’s few remaining natural tidal estuaries—a rare ecological habitat home to diverse wildlife. The plan threatens to degrade this critical site,

transforming it into a luxury amenity for wealthy tenants while offering no tangible benefit to the broader community. Additionally, the introduction of 1,200 mostly luxury units in an already overbuilt, under-resourced neighborhood would accelerate displacement, increase rents, and strain infrastructure—with no meaningful investment in transportation, schools, or public services. This development represents a betrayal of long-standing promises to the Greenpoint and Williamsburg communities. For two decades, residents have fought to see the waterfront preserved and made accessible, not handed over to private interests during a climate emergency.
